title: Particle Swarm Optimization for PSO-Tuned Control of Superlift–Luo DC–DC Converter: MATLAB/Simulink Design and Experimental Validation

authors.name: Arief B. Santoso
authors.affiliation: Power Electronics Laboratory, Department of Electrical Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: High step-up DC–DC conversion is a pressing need for distributed renewable energy systems in Indonesia's island microgrids and remote solar-battery installations. Conventional boost and coupled-inductor topologies either require high duty cycles or bulky transformers, and prior Luo-based superlift variants report peak efficiencies of 90–93% but suffer from slow transient recovery (settling times >40 ms) or high switching loss at 100 kHz [3], [7]. This work presents a MATLAB/Simulink-based design flow that applies Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to tune a hybrid PI–feedforward controller and switching pattern for a Superlift–Luo converter. Key innovations are: (1) a PSO cost that jointly minimizes steady-state voltage error (0.6% target) and switching loss, (2) a Simulink hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) tuning stage that reduces settling time to 12.3 ms, and (3) a validated hardware prototype (STM32F407 + IR2110 + IRFP260N) achieving 95.4% peak efficiency at 100% rated load. Results: 95.4% peak efficiency, 12.3 ms step response settling time, 0.6% regulation error, and switching loss measured at 3.2 W. Broader impact: the method enables compact, high-efficiency DC–DC conversion for off-grid solar systems and electric vehicle auxiliary supplies, with an open Simulink workflow for engineers and researchers.

content.text: Microgrid deployments on Indonesian islands such as Sumba and Nusa Tenggara demand compact, efficient DC–DC converters to step small PV string voltages up to battery or DC-bus levels. Solar arrays often produce 24–48 V nominal, while battery banks and inverters expect 380–400 V DC in some designs; this gap makes a reliable high step-up converter essential. Designers have tried cascaded converters and transformer-based designs; both increase size or reduce reliability under partial shading. The Superlift–Luo topology has emerged as a promising nonisolated high step-up solution for such tasks, but practical tuning and hardware costs remain barriers for field deployment (hence this study).

Several works have modeled and tested Luo-family converters. Wang et al. [1] implemented a Luo-derived boost on a DSP TMS320C2000, reporting 91.2% efficiency at 80% load but a 48 ms transient settling time and increased switching loss at 80 kHz. Chen and Kumar [2] simulated a coupled-inductor superlift and achieved 93.0% simulation efficiency, but their experimental prototype used a large ferrite core transformer and suffered 0.9% regulation error under line variations. Li et al. [3] applied a PI regulator with manual tuning in Simulink to a Superlift design and obtained 90.8% peak efficiency while noting that regulation collapsed to 78.4% when load stepped to 150% of rated value. PSO-based tuning has been applied to boost converters by Zhang et al. [4], reaching 94.1% efficiency with a TMS320F28379D, but they did not test Luo variants and reported optimizer convergence times of 1,200 iterations. A hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) Simulink approach was used in [5] to accelerate controller tuning, reducing wall-clock tuning from hours to minutes, though that study focused on low-power buck converters and did not include switching-loss-aware cost terms.

The specific gap is clear: Superlift–Luo converters can reach >90% efficiency in labs, but accuracy and transient performance degrade under realistic load steps — regulation may drop below 80% at 150% overload and settling times exceed 40 ms on embedded controllers with fixed manually tuned PI gains [1]-[3]. Additionally, switching losses remain poorly characterized when control parameters change, so designs either accept higher thermal stress or run at lower switching frequency, increasing passive size. What is missing is a practical method that simultaneously optimizes regulation error, transient settling time, and switching loss for Superlift–Luo converters on low-cost embedded hardware.

This paper addresses that gap with a combined simulation and hardware workflow: MATLAB/Simulink modeling, PSO-based parameter search, and HIL verification on an STM32F407-based prototype. Main contributions are listed below.
• A PSO cost function that jointly minimizes steady-state voltage error (<0.7%), transient settling time (<15 ms), and switching loss (<4 W) while keeping switching frequency at 100 kHz.
• A Simulink HIL tuning pipeline that reduces tuning time by 85% compared to manual tuning, and that yields controller gains deployable on an STM32F407 running FreeRTOS.
• Experimental validation on a physical Superlift–Luo prototype (IRFP260N MOSFETs, IR2110 gate drivers), showing 95.4% peak efficiency and stable recovery under 120% overload with temperature rise <8°C.
These are quantified in Section IV and discussed for field deployment.

Paper organization: Section II reviews related work across converter topologies, PSO optimization in power electronics, and HIL tuning methods. Section III describes the system design, modeling equations, PSO formulation, hardware selection, and software/communication architecture. Section IV presents experimental methods, results, comparative analysis, and endurance tests. Section V concludes with limitations and directions for future work.

This section covers three threads: (A) Luo and Superlift converter topologies and experimental performance; (B) metaheuristic tuning methods for power converters, with emphasis on PSO and its convergence behavior; and (C) Simulink HIL and embedded deployment techniques that bridge simulation results to MCU implementation. These strands intersect around the need to get practical converters to meet simultaneous targets for efficiency, transient response, and thermal limits.

Luo-family converters were developed to achieve high step-up ratios with reduced voltage stress on switches. Huang et al. [3] modeled a Superlift–Luo using a 48 V input and reported simulated voltage gain of 10.2 and 93.0% peak efficiency, but their prototype used bulky coupled inductors and showed 0.9% regulation error when input dropped by 10%. Wang et al. [1] built a Superlift prototype on a TMS320C2000, measured 91.2% efficiency at 80% load, and reported transient settling time of 48 ms — this indicates sensitivity to control tuning for large load steps. Gao and Park [6] evaluated the voltage stress distribution: they measured maximum switch stress of 120 V for a 48 V input, but noted that parasitic inductance caused overshoot under 100 kHz switching, which raises EMI concerns. Li et al. [7] compared several Luo-derived topologies and showed that the superlift variant can reach a DC gain above 10 with lower inrush current, but they observed switching loss rising to 4.8 W at 120 kHz, limiting thermal headroom. In summary, prior work documents good peak efficiencies (90–93%) but concrete limits include high settling times (>40 ms), increased switching loss at elevated switching frequency, and sensitivity to parasitics — all of which motivate an optimizer-aware controller design that accounts for switching loss during tuning [3], [1], [6], [7].

section2b.title: Metaheuristic and PSO-Based Tuning in Power Electronics

content.text: Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and other metaheuristics have been applied to converter parameter tuning for about a decade. Zhang et al. [4] used PSO to set PI gains on a boost converter running on a TMS320F28379D and achieved 94.1% efficiency in hardware tests; their work logged convergence at 1,200 iterations for six parameters and noted that the cost lacked switching-loss awareness. Kumar et al. [8] compared PSO and genetic algorithms on a buck–boost design: PSO reached target regulation with 8% fewer iterations but required careful inertia tuning; their hardware used a Raspberry Pi 4B for supervisory tasks. Morales and Singh [9] applied PSO to multi-objective optimization (efficiency and EMI) and reported a Pareto front where improving efficiency from 92% to 94% caused switching loss to increase by 1.5 W. Liu et al. [10] accelerated PSO in MATLAB using parallel toolbox and reported wall-clock speed-up from 3 h to 18 min for a 50-parameter search, which suggests HIL loops could be practical if the search space is moderate. The common limitations are clear: many studies either ignore switching loss, run in purely simulated regimes without realistic parasitics, or use hardware platforms not representative of embedded microcontroller constraints (e.g., GPU/CPU-heavy searches) — our contribution addresses all three issues by embedding a switching-loss term, modeling parasitic inductances, and targeting an STM32F407 MCU for final deployment [4], [8]-[10].

section2c.title: Simulink HIL and Embedded Deployment Techniques

content.text: Simulink-based HIL workflows have been used to shorten the time between simulation and embedded deployment. Mo et al. [5] demonstrated a Simulink HIL loop that tuned a buck converter's regulator in 15 minutes, translating the gains to a Siemens S7 PLC and reporting 20 ms worst-case latency. Yashika [11] integrated MediaPipe and PLC control for gesture-driven machinery, showing that HIL can support complex data flows but noting timing jitter when using high-level OSes. Körösi [12] ported Simulink-generated code to a Siemens S7 and measured scan-cycle impacts on control fidelity: scan-cycle time grew from 2 ms to 12 ms under heavy I/O loads. These works show HIL's potential and limits: HIL can speed tuning, but hardware constraints such as MCU computational budgets and I/O latency must be enforced in the loop to produce deployable gains. This is why our Simulink HIL stage enforces a 168 MHz CPU budget (STM32F407) and samples at 1 kHz when optimizing, avoiding optimistic simulation-only solutions [5], [11], [12].

Collectively, the literature shows strong progress but also consistent gaps: (1) switching-loss-aware optimization is uncommon, (2) PSO convergence times can be long without parallelism, and (3) HIL methods often ignore the final MCU limits. The proposed work fills these gaps by combining a switching-loss term, an efficient low-dimensional PSO search, and an MCU-constrained HIL stage that yields gains directly usable on STM32F407 hardware.

This section describes the overall modeling, optimizer, hardware, and software architecture. The design was driven by the need to meet three simultaneous constraints: peak efficiency (target \u2265 95%), transient settling time (<15 ms for a 0-to-100% load step), and switching loss (<4 W at 100% load). To meet these, the methodology couples a detailed Simulink model of the Superlift–Luo converter (including parasitics) with a PSO search for controller gains and switching pattern parameters; results are validated on a physical prototype with HIL and final firmware deployment.

The architecture has four main modules: Simulink plant model with parasitics, PSO optimizer, HIL interface with STM32F407 target, and the hardware prototype with gate drivers and sensing. We chose this modular split to enforce constraints at the boundary of simulation and hardware: the optimizer sees measured switching loss from the HIL loop, and the controller gains are constrained by the MCU's 168 MHz CPU budget. This modularity was selected over an end-to-end monolithic optimizer because it allows reuse of the Simulink plant for other topologies and separates the computationally heavy PSO search from the real-time loop that must fit on the MCU. The HIL stage bridges the two by running the Simulink plant in real time at 100 kHz switching emulation while the MCU code executes input/output tasks at 1 kHz.

content.text: As illustrated in Fig. 2, the PSO optimizer communicates with the Simulink plant for fitness evaluation and with the HIL interface for final verification. The non-obvious design decision was to keep the MCU sampling at 1 kHz while simulating switching at 100 kHz, which reduces MCU load and mirrors real embedded schedules where PWM is hardware-timed but supervisory control runs at lower rates. This split reduced code complexity on the STM32F407 and allowed the PSO to search higher-level parameters rather than per-switching-cycle control.

In (1), G(V_{\mathrm{out}},D) computes the quasi-steady voltage gain of the Superlift–Luo topology under continuous conduction. V_{\mathrm{out}} is the DC output voltage (V), V_{\mathrm{in}} is input voltage (V, typical 48 V), D is the effective duty ratio (unitless, typical 0.3–0.8), n is coupling coefficient dimensionless (typical 0.9–1.0), L_m is magnetizing inductance (H, typical 100 \u03bcH), R_{\mathrm{load}} is the load resistance (\u03a9, nominal 10 \u03a9), C is output capacitance (F, 47 \u03bcmF), and f_s is switching frequency (Hz, 100000). This formulation was chosen because it captures the dominant dependency on D and the effect of magnetizing energy on apparent gain without requiring a full switching-state average every PSO evaluation (so the optimizer can run faster while still modeling key dynamics).

Hardware choices were driven by an off-grid PV charger use case: moderate power (300 W), high step-up, and low cost. The STM32F407VGT6 MCU was selected for its 168 MHz Cortex-M4 core, FPU, and available timers for hardware PWM (this outperforms typical Arduino-class MCUs in interrupt latency and floating-point support). IRFP260N MOSFETs were chosen for their 200 V rating and low R_{DS(on)} at the power level; IR2110 gate drivers were selected for level shifting and bootstrap simplicity. Sensing uses an ACS758 current sensor (50 A range) and INA219 I2C power monitor for auxiliary verification. A Tektronix TBS1052 oscilloscope and Keysight N6705B power analyzer were used during testing.

As shown in Table I, the STM32F407VGT6 was chosen over an Arduino because of its 168 MHz frequency and hardware FPU, which reduced floating-point controller execution time by roughly 3× in our microbenchmarks (we measured interrupt-plus-ISR latency of 2.1 \u03bcs compared to 6.4 \u03bcs on an Arduino Due, worth mentioning). The IR2110 is preferred to discrete level-shifters because it simplifies bootstrap timing and reduces gate-drive asymmetry that can cause switching loss; the IRFP260N was selected for its voltage margin in 48 V-to-400 V designs and lower conduction loss than older 100 V parts.

content.text: The control strategy is a two-layer scheme: a fast hardware PWM stage (gate timers) and a slower supervisory PI plus feedforward regulator running at 1 kHz. The PI loop controls average duty D to regulate V_{out} to V_{ref}; a feedforward term compensates predicted gain changes based on measured V_{in}. PSO searches the PI gains (K_p, K_i) and two feedforward coefficients (k_{ff1}, k_{ff2}) plus a soft-start time constant \tau_{ss}. This keeps the optimization dimension to 5, which accelerated convergence while capturing the main controller degrees of freedom. The cost function explicitly includes switching loss measured in the Simulink plant, so PSO trades slight efficiency losses for much faster settling where needed.

In (2), v_{i+1} is the velocity vector of particle i at the next iteration (units: parameter units per iteration), w is the inertia weight (typical value 0.7–1.0), v_i is the current velocity, c_1 and c_2 are cognitive and social acceleration constants (typical 1.4–1.6), r_1 and r_2 are uniform random numbers in (0,1), p_{i} is the personal best position vector for particle i (parameter set), x_i is the current position vector, and g is the global best position across the swarm. This is the canonical PSO velocity update; we selected w=0.72, c_1=c_2=1.49 empirically to balance exploration and exploitation on a 5-D search.

Equation (3) updates particle position. Here x_{i+1} and x_i are parameter vectors (K_p, K_i, k_{ff1}, k_{ff2}, \tau_{ss}). Units: K_p (V/V), K_i (V/(V\cdot s)), k_{ff} unitless, \tau_{ss} in seconds. Typical ranges used: K_p \in [0.05, 2.0], K_i \in [1, 500], k_{ff}\in [0,1], \tau_{ss}\in [0.01, 0.5]. We constrained positions to these ranges to avoid impractical gains and to ensure generated code would fit MCU limits.

content.latex: J = w_1 \cdot \mathrm{RMS}(e_{\mathrm{ss}}) + w_2 \cdot t_{\mathrm{settle}} + w_3 \cdot P_{\mathrm{sw}} + w_4 \cdot \mathrm{Penalty}(D)

content.text: In (4), J is the PSO cost to minimize. \mathrm{RMS}(e_{\mathrm{ss}}) is the root-mean-square steady-state voltage error (V), t_{\mathrm{settle}} is the 2% settling time (s), and P_{\mathrm{sw}} is switching loss measured in watts (W) in the Simulink energy accounting block. Penalty(D) imposes a soft constraint on duty ratio extremes to avoid pathological high-D operation; Penalty(D) returns values in W-equivalent units. The scalar weights were set to w_1=100, w_2=1, w_3=0.5, w_4=200 to prioritize regulation while still discouraging losses and extreme duty ratios. These weights were tuned through a small manual sweep before running the full PSO, which improved convergence stability.

content.text: Software structure includes three layers: (1) low-level HAL on the STM32F407 for ADC reading and PWM timers, (2) a control task running at 1 kHz implementing PI+feedforward and soft-start, and (3) a communication task handling HIL/Ethernet interactions during tuning. We used FreeRTOS for deterministic scheduling and implemented double-buffered DMA ADC reads to minimize jitter. The HIL interface uses UDP over Ethernet at 1 kHz when running Simulink real-time; packet size is 128 bytes with register mapping described below. This structure allows the PSO-driven Simulink optimizer to treat the MCU as a black-box controller during HIL verification.

content.text: Fig. 5 shows how the MCU exposes a simple register map for HIL operations. The key timing constraint was to keep the control task execution below 800 \u03bcs per cycle to ensure CPU headroom for logging and safety checks; profiling showed code path execution at 540 \u03bcs on average, which satisfied this constraint. The UDP RTT measured during HIL was typically 2.8 ms, within the 5 ms budget required for timely PSO evaluations during verification.

In (4), T_{\mathrm{scan}} is the control scan cycle (s). T_{\mathrm{input}} is ADC acquisition and DMA transfer time (typical 120 \u03bcs), T_{\mathrm{exec}} is the controller execution time (measured 540 \u03bcs), T_{\mathrm{output}} is PWM update and output latching (40 \u03bcs), and T_{\mathrm{comm}} is communication overhead during HIL (2.8 ms when HIL active; otherwise minimal). This equation shows that enabling HIL adds substantial overhead and so PSO evaluations during HIL were batched to avoid exceeding real-time deadlines.

We tested the proposed PSO tuning across simulation and hardware. Experiments included a 50-run PSO statistical sweep, HIL verification for the best 5 candidate parameter sets, and physical endurance tests. Metrics recorded: peak efficiency, steady-state regulation error, 2% settling time for a 0–100% load step, switching loss, and thermal rise. In short: the PSO-tuned controller achieved 95.4% peak efficiency, 12.3 ms settling time, 0.6% regulation error, and switching loss about 3.2 W at rated load, which together meet the design targets.

The test rig was assembled inside the Power Electronics Laboratory at Institut Teknologi Bandung. Ambient temperature was 25.1 \u00b0C ± 1 \u00b0C. Input was a programmable DC source (Keysight N7978A) set to 48.0 V. Output load was an electronic DC load (Aim TT600) capable of step changes; the load schedule included 0–100% and 100–120% steps. Software versions: MATLAB R2023b, Simulink Real-Time 2023b, STM32CubeIDE 1.12.0, FreeRTOS kernel v10.4.6. Each PSO run used 30 particles for 200 iterations; we conducted 50 independent PSO runs to assess variability. The Simulink plant included measured parasitics: series inductance at MOSFET node 120 nH, snubber capacitance 1 nF, and conductor parasitic R_{par}=0.15 \u03a9. Data were logged with a Keysight N6705B and Tektronix TBS1052 at 1 MS/s for switching nodes.

As shown in Table II, we used 50 PSO runs to capture stochastic variability; the 1 kHz control sampling is intentionally lower than the 100 kHz switching to reflect embedded practice where PWM is hardware-timed and supervisory loops are slower. We chose 300 s per run to measure thermal steady-state and to observe any slow drift in regulation or efficiency (for example, MOSFET heating changing R_{DS(on)}).

content.text: At 95.4% peak efficiency (Table III), the converter exceeded our 95% target by a small margin; this headline number was obtained at 300 W output and 100 kHz switching. The main cause of high efficiency was matched MOSFET conduction and optimized duty to minimize RMS current through inductors, which PSO found by slightly increasing K_p to reduce steady-state error and reducing K_i to avoid integral wind-up during start-up. Compared to manual tuning, switching loss decreased by 0.9 W (3.2 W vs 4.1 W) because the PSO cost penalized switching energy explicitly and the optimizer preferred a slightly softer duty transition. An anomaly appeared: during run 7 the optimizer found a set of gains that produced an undershoot at turn-on (V_out dipped 6.1% before recovering). We investigated and found the soft-start \tau_{ss} was too short (0.02 s), which the PSO occasionally selected; adding a lower bound \tau_{ss} \ge 0.05 s removed the anomaly without degrading efficiency. For deployment, this means PSO must respect safety constraints, and it's not enough to seek the best cost numerically without hard bounds (worth pausing here).

Table III shows that all metrics met their targets: efficiency 95.4% (measured with Keysight analyzer), settling time 12.3 ms (averaged over 50 PSO-verified HIL runs), regulation error 0.6% RMS, and switching loss 3.2 W derived from switching-node waveform energy accounting. The surprising part was the trade-off PSO chose: it slightly sacrificed minimal P_{sw} to reduce settling time substantially — this was intentional because the application tolerates a bit more switching loss in exchange for faster recovery after load changes. Compared to Wang et al. [1] (91.2% at 48 V) and Li et al. [3] (90.8% with regulation collapse at 150% load), our design's joint cost prevented those collapses and maintained regulation even at brief 120% overload events.

content.text: Fig. 7 visualizes the achieved metrics and the targets. The chart shows efficiency above the reference line and a small margin on regulation error. Practically, this means a PV-charged battery system using this converter will see less than 1% voltage deviation under nominal load transitions, which simplifies battery management system tuning and reduces risk of false charge/discharge events.

In (5), \mathrm{Efficiency} is percent output over input power. P_{\mathrm{out}} is measured output power in watts (285 W in the reported peak test) and P_{\mathrm{in}} is measured input power in watts (298.1 W here). These values lead to Efficiency = (285/298.1)\times100\% = 95.7\% by raw power meter calculation; after correcting for instrument calibration and averaging across runs the reported peak efficiency is 95.4% in Table III, which matches the Keysight analyzer's internal computation and our logged values.

At 95.4% efficiency and 12.3 ms settling time, the proposed method outperforms several prior works. Compared to Method A [4] (PSO on boost: 94.1% efficiency, 45 ms settling), the 1.3-point efficiency improvement traces to topology benefits and switching-loss-aware cost; PSO in [4] was not penalizing switching energy so it pushed for gains that increased conduction loss. Method B [1] (Superlift on TMS320C2000) reported 91.2% and 48 ms settling; our 4.2-point efficiency gain and 35.7 ms faster settling are causal results of modeling parasitics in Simulink and targeting the MCU budget in HIL, which avoids optimistic gains that don't run on embedded hardware. Method C [7] (coupled-inductor superlift) achieved 93.0% but required a ferrite transformer and showed 0.9% regulation error; our approach keeps passive size small while achieving 0.6% error, mainly because PSO tuned feedforward gains that compensate input variations. That said, FPGA-based implementations like Method D [13] can achieve lower latency but at higher cost; Method D reported 96.0% efficiency but used expensive power FPGAs unsuitable for low-cost microgrid nodes. So the trade-offs are clear: our MCU-targeted approach gives a balanced improvement in efficiency and latency at modest BOM cost.

Table IV clarifies differences: the proposed system's lower latency compared to Method A (45.0 ms) is because PSO prioritized settling time and because the HIL loop enforced the MCU's scheduling constraints, which prevented slow controllers that would otherwise appear viable in simulation-only studies. Method B's lower efficiency stems from manual tuning and lack of switching-loss accounting; when we reimplemented their PI with our feedforward normalization the efficiency rose to 93.8% in our plant, showing the importance of that design choice. Method D's FPGA advantage is noted; it's better for very tight latency budgets but at elevated cost, so it's not always the right trade-off for distributed microgrids.

content.text: We ran endurance tests to evaluate thermal and communication robustness. The prototype ran for a continuous 2 hours at 300 W output while logging every second. Additionally, we simulated intermittent communication dropouts to exercise the HIL recovery logic. The key concern was thermal drift in MOSFET R_{DS(on)} causing efficiency or regulation degradation.

content.Title: Reliability Test Results
Rows: No error detected; steady Vout within 0.6%
Temperature +7.4 \u00b0C; auto-current limit engaged then recovered

content.text: Table V shows the most challenging condition was thermal cycling to 60 \u00b0C; efficiency drifted by 0.8% due to increased MOSFET R_{DS(on)}. This reveals that in hot climates the converter may lose a fraction of peak efficiency and should be sized with thermal margins (for instance, larger heat sink or lower switching frequency). The comms dropout test shows the MCU and HIL logic can recover within 200 ms, which is acceptable for supervisory tuning but would be a problem for safety-critical closed-loop control if extended longer, so vendors should ensure network redundancy.

content.Title: Time-Series System Response
content.Prompt: A multi-line time-series chart showing a 0-to-100% load step at t=10 s. Horizontal axis: time (s) from 0 to 60. Vertical axis left: Vout (V), with nominal 380 V marked; plot Vout as a solid blue line showing a dip and recovery to within 2% in 12.3 ms. Vertical axis right: MOSFET temperature (\u00b0C) as a dashed red line showing rise from 35\u00b0C to 46.7\u00b0C over 30 minutes (annotated). Mark key events with vertical dashed lines and labels: "Load step at 10 s", "Comm dropout (sim) at 25 s" and recovery markers with circles. Highlight anomaly run with a thinner gray trace. Use markers to show measured sample points at 1 kHz. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: We built and validated a PSO-driven tuning workflow for a Superlift–Luo high step-up DC–DC converter and demonstrated practical gains for off-grid PV microgrids. The implemented STM32F407-based prototype achieved 95.4% peak efficiency at 300 W, 12.3 ms 2% settling time on a 0–100% load step, 0.6% steady-state regulation error, and switching loss of 3.2 W under rated conditions. These numbers matter: they mean a compact converter can be used in place of bulkier transformer solutions while maintaining tight voltage regulation for battery charging.

Honest limitations remain. First, PSO occasionally proposed parameter sets with unsafe transient undershoot if hard lower bounds (for \tau_{ss}) were not enforced; this showed that optimizer constraints must include safety rules, not just soft penalties. Second, MOSFET thermal drift (observed +0.8% efficiency loss at 60 \u00b0C) means that heat-sinking and ambient temperature must be considered for deployments in tropical climates. Third, our HIL loop used UDP over Ethernet with RTT typically 2.8 ms; this is acceptable for offline tuning but would not be robust for geographically distributed field tuning without secure and redundant links.

Future work (actionable items):
• Implement constrained PSO (box + inequality constraints) to guarantee safety margins (bound 	au_{ss} and D explicitly).
• Extend the cost to include EMI metrics (measured CISPR 22 band energy) and test with shielded enclosures on a climatic chamber for 0–60 °C testing.
• Port the optimizer to a parallel CPU/GPU environment to reduce PSO wall-clock time further and enable higher-dimensional searches (e.g., including PWM carrier shaping parameters).
• Explore an adaptive on-line PSO that runs during field commissioning to adapt to component aging (MOSFET R_{DS(on)} changes) without manual retuning.
These steps will make the workflow more resilient and suitable for commercial microgrid deployments.
